head:
Action plans by profile · Ages 18 to 29

Young adult, 18 to 29: a realistic plan to get back or build your fitness

Being fit is neither easy nor hard. If you have decided to get started, it is not complicated. If you cannot manage to take action, it is very complicated, and that is not a lack of knowledge: everything is accessible. What it takes is patience and repeating the same gesture. This article is for those who stopped sport on leaving school, or never really started, and who are living through studies, a first job, a tight budget. It starts from what research says about this period, then offers twelve weeks with retests.

This is not a personal programme: that would need a person in front of you. It is the baseline plan, which looks much the same for almost everyone. What changes from one profile to another: the starting point, what to avoid, the dose, the real obstacles, the moment to ask for medical advice. The programme proposals are flagged: they have not been tested as they stand. The gains cited come from studies that were read.

The question

Take a typical portrait, illustrative and deliberately generic: someone aged 22, who does not exist. At school, he played sport: PE, a club, friends. Since starting higher education, nothing regular: a changing timetable, a limited budget, evenings out, irregular nights. He says “I'll start again on Monday”, resumes as he did at school, too hard and too often, with the idea that if it is not a proper one-hour session, it does not count. He lasts ten days, a busy week goes by, everything stops.

If you recognise yourself, this portrait is common, and research has a lot to say about it. It also corrects several received ideas: dropping out is less widespread than people think, it is not permanent, and the useful dose is smaller than those who give up imagine.

The question

Between 18 and 29, after years without regular practice, what really matters for getting back into shape, and how do you go about it when you have little time, little money and an unstable life?

What is at stake

Three stakes. First, what this decade builds: bone reaches its peak in the early or mid twenties, and aerobic capacity falls by about 1% a year without training.13 This is not a countdown, you can start again at 35 or 50, but it is easier and more rewarding now. Second, mood: 18-24 year olds are the age group in which self-reported depressive episodes rose the most in France between 2017 and 2021. Moving is not a treatment, but it is a support that has evidence, and limits. Finally, adherence, which decides the rest: the point is not to find the best programme, but to stick with one long enough for the body to respond. The demonstration follows five steps, from the general to the specific, then comes the plan.

Step 1 of 5 · What really changes after school

Activity falls modestly on average, but trajectories are very different

To check the starting idea, a Cambridge team (Corder and colleagues) combined 49 studies, out of 67 retained, that follow the same people between 13 and 30 years old. Moderate-to-vigorous activity is lower in adulthood by 5.2 minutes a day (95% interval: 3.1 to 7.3), about 13% of the starting value, and by 7.4 minutes with motion sensors. The authors call the decline “modest”.1 Winpenny and colleagues targeted the moment of life change: across 9 studies, leaving school goes with 7.04 fewer minutes a day (2.8 to 11.3), 16.35 in men, 6.61 in women with an interval that includes zero. Leaving university changed nothing on average (4 studies); starting work lowered activity in 2 studies out of 3.2,3

Leaving school costs a few minutes of effort a day, more for men

Bars: published mean differences (Corder et al., BJSM, 2019; Winpenny et al., Obesity Reviews, 2020). The last bar is greyed out: the published confidence interval includes zero, so we cannot say there is a decline in women in this review.1,2,3

What this means

Seven minutes a day make about 49 minutes a week (derived calculation), a third of the WHO minimum of 150 minutes: that is not nothing, and it is not a collapse. Above all, the heterogeneity between studies is huge (I² above 99%): the average hides very different trajectories. Your case is not written in advance.1

A counterpoint: in France, 79% of young men and 62% of young women aged 18-24 report meeting the activity recommendations, against 73% and 59% of all adults (2021 Barometer, 18-24 figures taken up by the CIDJ, second-hand, self-reported).6,7 The clear gap is in strength: 31% of adult men and 20% of adult women report meeting the muscle-strengthening recommendation (all ages).6

Cardio is mostly kept up, strength is the big absentee

Self-reported data, Santé publique France Barometer 2021 (BEH 2024, no. 12); the 18-24 figures come from a CIDJ article that takes up this Barometer (second-hand). Muscle strengthening is not broken down by age in the source read.6,7

What this means

The problem is often not “I no longer move”, but “I do nothing that looks like strength, and nothing regular”. A useful plan deals with both. These figures are self-reported, which generally overestimates actual practice.

The next question: does the level of activity at school predict today's level? If so, dropping out would be hard to make up.

Step 2 of 5 · Dropping out is not inevitable

Adolescent activity level only weakly predicts adult activity

A German study followed 947 young people (aged 11 to 17 at the start) for about six years. The correlation between starting activity and activity six years later is significant but weak: 0.21 for overall activity, 0.09 for leisure outside clubs. The authors speak of a “fluctuating variable”.5 A correlation of 0.2 corresponds to about 4% of variation explained (derived calculation). A Norwegian sensor study followed 731 children at 9 then 15 years old, and 258 of them at 24. Between 9 and 15, sedentary time rose by about 150 minutes a day; between 15 and 24, the changes are much smaller. Yet children in the least active quarter at 9 were about 1.9 times more likely to be in it again at 24 (odds ratio 1.88; 1.23 to 2.86), with measurements taken during the pandemic.4

What this means

In this cohort, most of the drop-off happens before age 15, and tendencies persist somewhat. But nothing says that someone who stopped at 18 is “finished”: a weak correlation leaves room for change. These are group averages, not an individual prognosis.

If the past does not dictate what follows, what is at stake in the coming years?

Step 3 of 5 · What this period builds

Bone, aerobic capacity, strength: reserves that are built or lost

Bone. The National Osteoporosis Foundation press release (2016) places peak bone mass “in the early twenties”, the IOF compendium “around the mid twenties”. The NOF estimates that lifestyle influences 20 to 40% of adult peak, with level A evidence for calcium and physical activity.11,12 The window does not close all at once: in women aged 35 to 45, impact exercises still gave a modest gain at the femoral neck (1.6% against 0.6% in controls).12 (Taken from our article “Bone: a capital”.)

Aerobic capacity. In the CARDIA study, more than 4,400 young American adults aged 18 to 30 took a treadmill stress test, then were followed for 15 years. According to the university press release, low or moderate fitness went with about twice the risk of diabetes or metabolic syndrome compared with high fitness, and improving fitness over 7 years with up to 50% lower risk.10 This is an association, read from a press release.

Strength. In adults, muscle strengthening goes with a risk of death 0.85 times that of non-practitioners, and combining strength plus aerobic activity with 0.60 times that of people who do neither.14 These are not young adults: this shows what is at stake over the long term, not what awaits you at 25.

What this means

This period builds reserves: bone, aerobic capacity, muscle. It is not a medical emergency, it is a margin that will make it simpler to start again at 40. The argument is not fear of a disease in thirty years: the same repeated effort probably has more effect when the body still responds well (reasoning, not a study result).

What remains is how much effort and of what type. The benchmarks are more modest than you might think.

Step 4 of 5 · How much and what: the baseline plan is shared

The baseline dose is the same for everyone, and strength and cardio combine

The 2020 WHO guidelines for ages 18-64 recommend 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week (or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity), plus muscle strengthening on at least two days a week. A little is better than nothing, and sessions of any length now count: the old rule of a 10-minute minimum has gone.16 For mood, the dose study by Pearce (15 studies, 191,130 adults) associates half the recommended dose with a depression risk about 18% lower, and the full dose with 25% lower (self-reported activity, association).25

Do strength and endurance interfere with each other? In a 2022 review (Schumann, 43 studies, 1,090 participants), combined training does not differ from strength alone for muscle mass and maximal strength. For power (jumping, sprinting), there is a small disadvantage, especially when both are in the same session, and more so with at least three hours between them.15 The quality of the studies is moderate (4.3 out of 10).

Finally, a small dose can already produce a measurable effect. In the Gillen trial (2016), 25 sedentary men aged about 27 did 12 weeks of three sessions: about 10 minutes of intervals (three all-out 20-second sprints) or about 50 minutes of continuous moderate effort. Peak VO2 rose by 19% in both groups, with about five times less time for the intervals.21

Three ten-minute interval sessions gave the same gain in aerobic capacity as three fifty-minute sessions

Gillen et al., PLoS ONE, 2016: 25 sedentary men (mean age 27), 9 in intervals, 10 in continuous effort, 6 controls. Very small trial, supervised cycling sessions, maximal effort on the sprints: not transferable as it stands to someone who has not been assessed or supervised.21

What this means

Lack of time is not an absolute obstacle: there is a minimal version that works, and it helps you keep going through busy weeks. Do not conclude, however, that “ten minutes is enough”: the trial measures aerobic capacity and insulin sensitivity, not strength or bone, and the dose for health remains the WHO's.

The baseline plan is set: a little regular cardio, strength twice a week, gentle progression. Most people already know this. What remains is what really blocks you.

Step 5 of 5 · What really blocks you

Habit, all-or-nothing, student life and mood

Habit is counted in weeks

The study by Lally (University College London) followed 96 volunteers, students with a mean age of 27 (82 finished), who repeated a behaviour every day for 84 days. Maximum automaticity is reached in 66 days on average, with a range from 18 to 254 days (predicted value). Exercise took about 1.5 times longer than drinking a glass of water or eating a piece of fruit. A missed day had little effect: it is repeated lapses that reduce the level reached.17

A habit takes more than two months on average, and differences between people are huge

Lally et al., 2010, based on the British Psychological Society write-up. Values beyond 84 days are model estimates, not observations.17

What this means

If it does not become easy after three weeks, that is normal. And missing a day breaks nothing: what breaks it is deciding that everything is lost.

Two tools have evidence. “If-then” planning (“if it is Tuesday at 18h, then I go out for twenty minutes”) has a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals: 94 tests, d = 0.65.18 Monitoring your own behaviour is the technique that explains the most about differences between interventions (122 evaluations, 44,747 participants); combined with another self-regulation technique, the effect is 0.42 against 0.26.19 These studies cover activity and diet, not only young adults.

All-or-nothing

In a recent qualitative study (Segar and colleagues, 4 focus groups, 27 adults aged 19 to 79 including students, who had failed to keep up regular practice), when the plan could not be followed to the letter, they preferred to do nothing rather than adapt it. Many demanded 45 or 60 minutes or a high effort, and judged that walking or doing a short session did not “count”.20 Small sample, no figures: a signal, not a measurement. It nonetheless describes your typical portrait, and the guidelines have changed: every duration counts.16

Sleep, alcohol, budget

Sleep. A meta-analysis of 77 studies (Craven, 2022) finds that acute sleep deprivation reduces strength a little (about 2.85%) and strength endurance more (about 9.85%, imprecise estimate).23 One bad night therefore does not cancel a session: shorten it. In France, women aged 18 to 29 sleep 7 h 53 on average, the longest duration of the groups detailed: the problem may be irregularity, which these sources do not measure.9

Alcohol. In a crossover trial of 8 active men (Parr, 2014), about 12 standard drinks after a mixed session reduced muscle protein synthesis by 24% (with protein) to 37% (with carbohydrate) compared with protein alone.22 This is the dose of a very big night out and a tiny sample: it is not the measure of one drink. The studies read do not allow anything more precise about an acceptable dose.

Budget. No study read compares the gym with training at home, so we do not claim it. Useful doses are modest, walking and running cost nothing, and the jumps that load bone need no equipment. The plan below therefore requires no equipment (proposal).

Mood

Between 2017 and 2021, the share of 18-24 year olds reporting a depressive episode in the year rose from 11.7% to 20.8%, the largest increase of the age groups; among 18-75 year olds, from 9.8% to 13.3%.8 Sport is associated with less depression (study of 1.2 million people, self-reported activity),24 and trials show on average a moderate drop in symptoms (index 0.4 to 0.5, 2023 review of reviews). But Cochrane notes that the effect becomes uncertain with only the most rigorous trials (0.18, indistinguishable from zero).26,27 It is a support, not a replacement for treatment; and training too much relative to recovery can worsen mood.28

What this means

When your mood is low, start with half the dose and with short sessions. If sadness, anxiety or lack of motivation last several weeks or get in the way of your studies or your work, talk to a doctor or a health professional. If you have suicidal thoughts, 3114 answers 24 hours out of 24, free and confidential; in case of immediate danger, call 15 or 112.35

The twelve-week action plan

Proposal, not tested as such. Durations, frequencies and progression rules are built from the benchmarks read (WHO, Pearce, Schumann, Lally, Gillen). No trial has tested this programme. It is aimed at an adult aged 18 to 29 with no known illness or symptom.

Phase 0: before you start

Screening. The PAR-Q+ (in France, the Q-AAP+ cited by the HAS) has seven questions: if you answer no to all of them, you can start gradually; otherwise, you complete the rest and discuss it with a health professional.32,34 According to the ACSM (2015), someone who does not train, with no signs or known disease, does not need prior medical advice: you start with light to moderate effort and add vigorous effort gradually. If there are signs suggestive of cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, advice is recommended.33 The HAS notes “almost no contraindication” to moderate activity.34

Starting test. Do the THW endurance and strength tests, in reproducible conditions (same time of day, same equipment, same warm-up). The mobility or balance test is not essential for this profile: do it if you have discomfort or stiffness.

Two decisions. Set two strength slots and three cardio slots, written as “if, then” (“if it is Monday and Thursday at 18h, then strength at home”). Define your floor version: the minimum session (for example 10 minutes) done even in busy weeks. A busy week means the floor version, never zero.

Volume that rises in steps, three retests and a floor version for busy weeks

Programme proposal (heights are proportional to minutes). Weekly totals: 150, 200 and 240 minutes. Retests take place at weeks 4, 8 and 12. The cardio minutes of phase 3 (150) reach the bottom of the WHO range; those of phase 1 (90) represent 60% of it.16

Phase 1: weeks 1 to 4, setting the rhythm (about 150 min per week)

Strength, 2 sessions of 30 minutes. Whole body: leg bend (squat, standing up from a chair), hip hinge (glute bridge), push (incline push-ups), pull (resistance-band row), plank. Three sets of 8 to 12 repetitions, keeping two or three repetitions in reserve. The aim is to learn the movements: you should be able to carry on the next day.

Cardio, 3 sessions of 30 minutes. Brisk walking, cycling or run-walk alternation, at an intensity where you speak in short sentences. Add a few sets of 10 small jumps at the end of the warm-up for bone (proposal based on impact trials, not done in young adults).

Retest, week 4. Redo the THW endurance and strength tests, in the same conditions as the starting test, replacing one session. Compare with your own first result, not with someone else's. Avoid testing after a bad night or when you are tired.

To move on to phase 2: at least 4 sessions out of 5 for two weeks in a row, with no pain lasting more than 48 hours (proposal). Otherwise, stay one more week: it costs nothing.

Phase 2: weeks 5 to 8, building gently (about 200 min per week)

Strength, 2 sessions of 40 minutes. Same structure, with more load or a harder variant (standard push-ups, Bulgarian split squat, a harder band). When 12 repetitions are clean on all sets, add a repetition or change the variant.

Cardio, 3 sessions of 40 minutes. Two easy, one with intervals (six times one fast minute, one and a half minutes easy, after a 10-minute warm-up). This is a gentle version, not Gillen's sprint protocol.

Retest, week 8. Same protocol. To step back a level (proposal): two weeks in a row under 3 sessions out of 5, sleep that clearly worsens, pain that persists, or fatigue that rises while training increases.

Phase 3: weeks 9 to 12, consolidating (about 240 min per week)

Strength, 2 sessions of 45 minutes (or 3 of 30), with one more set or variant per exercise. When possible, separate strength and cardio by another day or at least three hours: it is in this case that the slight disadvantage for power disappears (step 4). Cardio, about 150 minutes in three or four sessions, including one with intervals: the bottom of the WHO range. Retest, week 12, same protocol. The gains in the trials are an order of magnitude, not a target.

After week 12: maintain and choose

Keep the core: 2 strength sessions and 3 cardio sessions, that is 150 to 240 minutes. Retake the tests about every three months, or when your life changes (internship, first job, moving). In busy weeks, floor version. Then you can specialise: team sport, running, hybrid goal, starting again from a phase 1 for that new aspect.

Starting again after a break: detraining and injuries

In recently trained people, VO2max falls by 3.6 to 6% after 2 to 4 weeks of stopping, and general strength is largely kept up to 4 weeks (Mujika and Padilla, 2000).29 In a trial of 14 young men (Ogasawara, 2013), cycles of 6 weeks of training and 3 weeks off gave muscle and strength gains comparable to 24 continuous weeks: the gains lost during the break came back quickly.30 These results concern breaks of a few weeks; we have no data read on breaks of several years.

For injuries, a Dutch trial (Buist, 2008, 532 novice runners) finds 20.8% injured with a graded 13-week programme (10% rule) and 20.3% with a standard 8-week programme: no significant difference.31 About one beginner in five gets injured within a few weeks, and one arithmetic rule did no better than another. Hence the criteria: start low, rise in short steps, listen to pain (proposal).

Common mistakes, warning signs, when to see someone

  • Starting everything at once.This is the scenario of the portrait: ten intense days, then nothing. Start at a dose you would keep up even when tired.
  • Doing only cardio, or only strength.Both are useful and compatible; strength is what few people do.
  • Compensating with excess.If sleep and mood fall while you are doing more, ease off.28

When to stop and see someone. Screening questionnaires refer you to a professional from certain positive answers, and the ACSM asks you to stop and seek advice if signs appear during training.32,33 The sources read do not detail these signs; common-sense benchmarks (not from these sources) are chest pain or discomfort, feeling faint, breathlessness unrelated to the effort, unusual palpitations, a family history of sudden death at a young age to be mentioned before starting. Muscle or joint pain that lasts more than a few days also warrants advice.

The frank answer

What really matters for getting back into shape between 18 and 29, with little time, money and stability?

Solid. Activity falls modestly on average after school, with very different trajectories. Adolescent level only weakly predicts adult level: nothing is settled. Official recommendations are clear (150 to 300 minutes of aerobic activity, two days of strength, any duration counts), and strength is the point where most adults fall short. A habit takes more than two months on average and tolerates a lapse; “if, then” planning and monitoring have a demonstrated effect on average.

Probable. Combining strength and cardio does not hold back muscle or maximal strength. A modest dose is associated with benefits, including for mood. Building reserves at this age rests on associations and on data from children or older adults.

Proposal. The twelve-week programme, its steps, its criteria for moving forward and stepping back, the floor version and the retest calendar: consistent with the data read, never tested as they stand, and they replace neither a doctor, nor a coach in case of injury, illness or a specific goal.

Not demonstrated. The effect of alcohol at student-life doses, the comparison of gym and home, returning after several years off, the effect of this programme in young adults.

The lever is therefore not a programming secret. It is deciding on a dose you can sustain, repeating it for more than two months, measuring what changes, and not stopping because one week was missed.

Limitations
  • The studies describe group averages, often with self-reported activity and very high heterogeneity.
  • Many of the benefits cited (mortality, diabetes, mood) are associations, not demonstrated causes.
  • Several trials are very small (8 to 25 people) and mostly recruit men.
  • Some sources were read from a summary, a press release or a write-up: the editorial note lists which.
  • Nothing here is personalised medical advice.

Frequently asked questions

Is the plan different for a woman and for a man?

The baseline plan is the same. On average, according to the studies read, the drop in activity on leaving school is larger in men, and women less often report meeting the strengthening recommendation (20% against 31%, all adults). These are averages, which say nothing about your case.

What if I miss a week?

Resume at the level you were at, or one level lower if you were ill. A missed day has little effect on a habit, and a few weeks off do not lose you most of your strength.17,29

How long before I see a result?

In the small Gillen trial, peak VO2 had risen by 19% in 12 weeks in sedentary men.21 A habit settles in around 66 days on average.17 At the retest, expect progress mainly in strength at first, because the movements are being learned: this is a reasonable expectation, not a promised result.
